cases.title: Documentation Integrity and Late Charting
cases.stem: During a hectic shift, a nurse forgets to document that a PRN pain medication was administered at 1400. At 1630, while reviewing the chart, the nurse considers entering the note as if it were documented in real time because “that’s easier and it still happened.” The patient is currently comfortable, and a second nurse is preparing to assess for another PRN dose. The nurse recognises that documentation must be accurate, timely, and honest. The record must reflect what happened without falsifying the time or sequence of care. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Documentation Integrity and Late Charting | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which facts make this a documentation issue? Select all that apply.

options.text: Another dose may be considered soon
The nurse is considering charting as if it were done earlier
The medication was given but not charted at the time
The patient is currently comfortable
Accurate medication timing matters for safety

questions.rationale: All these facts are relevant. Documentation timing affects medication safety and legal accuracy. Comfort does not remove the need for honest charting. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Documentation Integrity and Late Charting | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Late charting means the event should not be documented at all
Backdating the entry as if charted in real time is acceptable if the medication was actually given
Timing does not matter for PRN medications
The medication still must be documented, but the entry must accurately reflect that it is a late entry

questions.rationale: Late entries should be documented honestly according to policy. Falsifying time compromises the integrity of the record and may endanger the patient if repeat doses are considered. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Documentation Integrity and Late Charting | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Finishing charting quickly regardless of accuracy
Ensuring safe and truthful medication documentation so further dosing decisions are accurate
Protecting the nurse from embarrassment
Avoiding unit discussion

questions.rationale: Accurate medication records protect patient safety and legal accountability. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Documentation Integrity and Late Charting | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Enter the medication administration as a late entry according to policy and inform relevant staff if dosing decisions may be affected
Omit the record entirely because it is late
Ask another nurse to chart it under their login
Change the time to make the chart look neat

questions.rationale: The nurse must chart honestly and communicate if the omitted documentation could affect patient care or additional dosing. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Documentation Integrity and Late Charting | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clarify for the next nurse or provider exactly when the medication was actually given
Follow facility policy for late entries and corrections
Reflect on workflow changes needed to reduce repeat omissions
Assume the omission has no effect because the patient is comfortable
Reassess the patient’s current pain status

questions.rationale: All these actions support professional documentation integrity and patient safety. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Documentation Integrity and Late Charting | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The documentation is altered to appear on time
The record accurately reflects the late entry, the timing is clear to the team, and future medication decisions remain safe
No correction is made because the patient is comfortable
The second PRN dose is given without knowing the first dose timing

questions.rationale: Effective management preserves both record integrity and clinical safety.

cases.title: Confidentiality and Family Information Requests
cases.stem: Ms. Asha Patel, a competent adult patient, has been admitted for treatment of a newly diagnosed STI. She tells the nurse privately, “Please do not discuss my diagnosis with my parents. I’m not ready.” Later that day, her mother arrives, states that she helps with all medical decisions, and demands to know exactly why Asha is in hospital. She says, “I am her mother, so I have the right to know.” The nurse must balance family pressure with patient confidentiality and the patient’s expressed wishes. The situation requires calm, respectful, legally appropriate communication. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Confidentiality and Family Information Requests | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings are most relevant in deciding what information can be shared? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient explicitly requested privacy
The mother is demanding details
Family involvement does not automatically create access rights
The patient is a competent adult
The diagnosis is sensitive health information

questions.rationale: All of these are important. Competent adult patients control who receives their information unless they provide permission or other legal exceptions apply. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Confidentiality and Family Information Requests | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Sensitive diagnoses should be hidden from the chart entirely
Parents always have full access to adult children’s medical information
The nurse may share limited details because the mother seems concerned
The patient’s confidentiality must be respected unless the patient authorizes disclosure or another legal basis exists

questions.rationale: Concern does not equal authorization. The nurse must protect the patient’s confidentiality and right to privacy. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Confidentiality and Family Information Requests | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Protecting the patient’s confidentiality while communicating professionally with the family
Giving the mother enough information to keep peace
Avoiding an awkward conversation with the mother
Finishing other tasks first and leaving the mother waiting indefinitely

questions.rationale: The nurse’s priority is to uphold confidentiality while remaining respectful and calm. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Confidentiality and Family Information Requests | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Explain respectfully that patient information cannot be shared without the patient’s permission and offer to support a conversation if the patient agrees
Disclose the diagnosis because family support is important
Ignore the mother completely
Tell the mother the diagnosis off the record

questions.rationale: The nurse should set a professional boundary, protect confidentiality, and offer a supportive pathway only if the patient consents. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Confidentiality and Family Information Requests | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume family relationship overrides confidentiality
Encourage the patient to decide if and when she wants family involved
Confirm the patient’s preferences about who may receive information
Avoid discussing the case in public or with unauthorized individuals
Document relevant confidentiality preferences if appropriate

questions.rationale: These actions reinforce privacy and patient autonomy. Family relationship alone does not override a competent adult’s confidentiality. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Confidentiality and Family Information Requests | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The patient’s privacy is preserved, family communication remains respectful, and any disclosure occurs only with patient consent
The staff discuss the STI at the nurses’ station within family hearing range
The mother is given information because she insists loudly enough
The patient’s wishes are ignored to reduce conflict

questions.rationale: Effective management protects confidentiality while preserving professionalism and trust.

cases.title: Scope of Practice and LPN Assignment Decision
cases.stem: An RN is supervising care on a step-down unit with an LPN and a UAP available. One patient needs a comprehensive admission assessment, another requires reinforcement of teaching after the RN’s initial education, a third is stable and needs routine oral medications, and a fourth has just returned from the operating room with worsening pain and dropping blood pressure. The charge nurse asks the RN to organise assignments quickly. The RN must use role clarity to determine what can be safely assigned to the LPN and what remains RN-only responsibility. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Scope of Practice and LPN Assignment Decision | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which factors are central when assigning to an LPN? Select all that apply.

options.text: Whether initial teaching or evaluation is required
Whether the task requires comprehensive assessment
Need for complex judgment in a deteriorating patient
Routine medication administration for a stable patient
Patient stability

questions.rationale: All these factors matter. LPN roles vary by jurisdiction, but NCLEX-style delegation questions emphasize that comprehensive assessment, initial teaching, and unstable patients generally remain RN responsibilities. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Scope of Practice and LPN Assignment Decision | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Initial admission assessments are always ideal for UAPs
Stable routine care and some reinforcement tasks may be assigned appropriately, but RN judgment tasks must remain with the RN
The RN has no accountability once the assignment is given
The LPN may independently manage the post-operative unstable patient because the unit is busy

questions.rationale: The RN must match task complexity and patient stability to role scope while remaining accountable for the delegation decision. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Scope of Practice and LPN Assignment Decision | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which task is safest to assign to the LPN?

options.text: Interpretation of new hypotension and pain deterioration without RN involvement
Routine oral medications for the stable patient and reinforcement after prior RN teaching if appropriate to local scope
Initial comprehensive admission assessment
Independent management of the unstable post-operative patient

questions.rationale: Routine care for stable patients is generally more appropriate for LPN assignment. Initial assessments and unstable patient evaluation remain RN responsibilities. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Scope of Practice and LPN Assignment Decision | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the RN do first?

options.text: Avoid assigning anything because delegation is risky
Assign the most complex case to the LPN to save time
Assign based on scope and stability, keeping unstable assessment/evaluation duties with the RN and giving clear direction for delegated tasks
Let the LPN choose whichever patient seems easiest

questions.rationale: The RN should actively organize care according to patient need, scope, and accountability. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Scope of Practice and LPN Assignment Decision | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume the LPN can substitute for full RN clinical judgment in all cases
Clarify what findings the LPN should report immediately
Reassess outcomes of delegated care as needed
Personally assess the unstable post-operative patient without delay
Ensure reinforcement teaching is based on the RN’s initial teaching plan

questions.rationale: These actions reflect safe assignment and supervision. The RN retains responsibility for assessment, interpretation, and evaluation. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Scope of Practice and LPN Assignment Decision | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective assignment and supervision?

options.text: Stable tasks are completed appropriately within role scope, the unstable patient is assessed promptly by the RN, and key findings are communicated clearly
The LPN independently manages the unstable patient’s hypotension with no RN involvement
Admission assessment is omitted due to poor assignment planning
No one knows who is responsible for follow-up

questions.rationale: Effective team management depends on safe role allocation, supervision, and clear communication.

cases.title: Impaired Practice and Substance Use by a Nurse
cases.stem: On a night shift, a nurse notices that a colleague smells strongly of alcohol, has bloodshot eyes, and nearly drops a narcotic vial while preparing medications. The colleague insists they are “just exhausted” and asks the nurse not to say anything because they are short-staffed. The impaired nurse then attempts to care for a sedated patient receiving high-risk opioids. The observing nurse feels conflicted, knowing that reporting could affect the colleague’s career. However, patient safety and professional duty are at stake. The nurse must act within legal-ethical expectations and workplace policy. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Impaired Practice and Substance Use by a Nurse | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings suggest possible impaired practice? Select all that apply.

options.text: Difficulty handling narcotic medication
Request to keep the concern secret
Bloodshot eyes and poor coordination
Smell of alcohol
Working with high-risk sedated patients

questions.rationale: All these findings raise serious concern for impaired practice. The request for secrecy is especially concerning because it places patient safety below personal protection. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Impaired Practice and Substance Use by a Nurse | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The colleague may be impaired and must be removed from patient care through proper reporting channels
Staffing shortage means the concern should be ignored
Fatigue alone always explains alcohol odor
The narcotic near-miss is unrelated to safety

questions.rationale: The nurse’s duty is to protect patients. Potential impairment requires immediate action through appropriate supervisory processes. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Impaired Practice and Substance Use by a Nurse | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Avoiding extra documentation
Immediate patient safety risk from possible impaired nursing practice
Protecting the colleague from embarrassment
Preventing staffing inconvenience

questions.rationale: Patient safety is the priority. Professional accountability includes reporting unsafe practice. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Impaired Practice and Substance Use by a Nurse | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Notify the appropriate supervisor immediately and ensure the colleague is removed from direct patient care pending assessment
Personally cover for the colleague and say nothing
Publicly accuse the colleague in front of patients
Ignore the issue until the end of the shift

questions.rationale: The nurse should act promptly and through the correct chain of command. Public confrontation is not the safest or most professional first step. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Impaired Practice and Substance Use by a Nurse | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Document objective observations if required by policy
Assume friendship or sympathy overrides duty to report
Focus on observed behaviours rather than assumptions or gossip
Protect patients receiving high-risk medications from delayed monitoring
Cooperate with formal review or occupational health processes

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate professional responses. Objectivity and patient safety are essential. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Impaired Practice and Substance Use by a Nurse | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The impaired practice concern is escalated promptly, patient care is reassigned safely, and the issue is handled through policy-based processes
The colleague continues high-risk care because the unit is short-staffed
Documentation is avoided because the issue feels uncomfortable
Staff agree informally to keep the problem quiet

questions.rationale: Effective management protects patients immediately and addresses the concern through formal professional channels.

cases.title: Cultural Beliefs, Advocacy, and Ethical Communication
cases.stem: Mrs. Noor Rahman is a 45-year-old patient admitted with uncontrolled diabetes. The care team recommends insulin initiation, but she states through an interpreter that she wants to speak with her husband and elder family members first because health decisions in her family are made collectively. A frustrated staff member says, “She is refusing treatment. Just make her sign refusal forms now.” The nurse recognises that culturally responsive care requires respect, clarification, and patient-centred advocacy rather than assuming noncompliance. At the same time, the nurse must ensure that the patient understands her condition and the consequences of delaying treatment. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Cultural Beliefs, Advocacy, and Ethical Communication | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings are most important in this cultural-ethical situation? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient wants family involvement in decision-making
Insulin treatment is clinically important
An interpreter is needed for accurate communication
The patient may need more time and explanation
Staff are labeling the patient as noncompliant too quickly

questions.rationale: All these cues matter. Cultural decision-making practices should be respected while ensuring the patient still receives accurate information and has the opportunity to make an informed decision. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Cultural Beliefs, Advocacy, and Ethical Communication | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Family involvement means the patient loses all autonomy
Cultural beliefs are irrelevant in hospital practice
The patient is automatically refusing treatment and should be pressured immediately
The nurse should support culturally sensitive communication, clarify understanding, and avoid premature labeling

questions.rationale: The patient is not necessarily refusing treatment; she may be requesting culturally meaningful consultation. The nurse should not confuse culturally shaped decision-making with simple noncompliance. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Cultural Beliefs, Advocacy, and Ethical Communication | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Avoiding interpreter use to save time
Ensuring informed, respectful communication while protecting the patient’s right to participate in care decisions
Letting the family decide without including the patient
Ending the conversation quickly for staff convenience

questions.rationale: The priority is ethically sound communication that respects culture and patient rights while still addressing health risks. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Cultural Beliefs, Advocacy, and Ethical Communication | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Pressure the patient to sign refusal forms immediately
Speak only to the husband because the family is involved
Stop all discussion of treatment until discharge
Use the interpreter appropriately, clarify the patient’s understanding, and explore how family involvement can occur without compromising informed care

questions.rationale: The nurse should facilitate respectful, accurate communication. Using a qualified interpreter and exploring the patient’s preferences are key advocacy steps. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Cultural Beliefs, Advocacy, and Ethical Communication | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Advocate against dismissive labeling by staff
Assume that culturally based hesitation means the patient does not understand anything
Respect cultural beliefs while still explaining clinical risks clearly
Distinguish between delayed decision-making and true informed refusal
Document the patient’s preferences and discussions accurately

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate. Cultural sensitivity does not mean abandoning education; rather, it means providing it respectfully and effectively. Program Area: Professional Practice and Ethics | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Cultural Beliefs, Advocacy, and Ethical Communication | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective nursing advocacy?

options.text: The patient receives accurate information through appropriate communication, cultural preferences are respected, and treatment decisions are made with informed participation
Staff pressure the patient into signing refusal forms without interpreter support
The family speaks for the patient while the patient is excluded
Cultural concerns are ignored because insulin is important

questions.rationale: Effective advocacy balances respect, informed decision-making, and professional communication without stereotyping or coercion.
